issues.legal_issue: A court may consider a private-defence plea that arises from the evidence even when the accused did not formally plead it.
material_facts: The appellants did not raise private defence in their statements under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The basis for the plea had been put forward in cross-examination and supported by defence evidence.
issues.conclusion: The court could consider the private-defence plea on the material in the record; the accused bore the burden of establishing it on a preponderance of probabilities.
issues.legal_principle: An accused need not formally plead private defence if it arises from the evidence on record. The accused may discharge the burden by showing a preponderance of probabilities from that material. The Court relied on In re Jogali Bhaigo Naiks and another.

predicates.criminal_case: The matter is a criminal prosecution in which the accused relies on private defence.
predicates.private_defence_basis_in_evidence: The accused presents evidence or elicited testimony that supplies a factual basis for private defence.

issues.definition: When a criminal case contains evidence supporting private defence, the court may consider that defence.

issues.legal_issue: A managing officer cannot effect a statutory eviction from property that has left the officer’s control, or use the statutory eviction power without its required prior steps.
material_facts: A sale certificate had been issued to the purchaser before the purported delivery of possession.
The tenant had remained in possession, and the record did not show that the tenant’s tenancy had been terminated.
The managing officer issued a delivery warrant after the government’s interest in the property had been alienated.
No action under the preliminary parts of the statutory eviction process had been taken against the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The managing officer lacked authority to evict the tenant in the circumstances; the purported delivery had no legal effect, and the tenant remained in possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(1)–(3) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 applies to property under the control of a managing officer or managing corporation. The power under subsection (3) is special and may be exercised only in accordance with its prescribed conditions, including the prior steps under subsections (1) and (2). A tenant ordinarily must be evicted through a court of competent jurisdiction after termination of the tenancy. The Court relied on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and others.

rule.if: sale_certificate_issued and tenant_remained_in_possession and property_left_officer_control and required_prior_eviction_steps_absent

predicates.sale_certificate_issued: A purchaser received a sale certificate for the property before the purported administrative delivery.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_possession: A tenant continued to occupy the property and the tenancy had not been shown to have ended.
predicates.property_left_officer_control: The property had been alienated so that it was no longer under the managing officer’s control.
predicates.required_prior_eviction_steps_absent: The managing officer had not taken the prescribed preliminary steps against the occupant before attempting eviction.

issues.definition: A purported administrative delivery has no legal effect when a tenant remains in possession after the property has left the officer’s control and the required prior eviction steps were not taken.

issues.legal_issue: A person may use necessary force to defend another’s property against an immediate forcible intrusion when the defender is protecting possession that has not been lawfully displaced.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the field for many years and remained in possession because the purported administrative delivery was ineffective.
The purchaser and his companions came to the field with a tractor to assert possession after previously seeking to obtain possession from the tenant.
The tenant and the appellants were unaware of the purported delivery, and the tenant’s companions were taken by surprise by the attempted entry.
The purchaser’s group included a person carrying an unlicensed pistol, and the appellants intervened to protect the tenant’s possession.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to prevent the purchaser’s group from taking possession by using necessary force.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 97 of the Indian Penal Code, a person may defend their own or another person’s property against criminal trespass, subject to section 99, including its limits on necessity and the amount of harm inflicted. A person in settled possession may defend it even against the rightful owner until evicted in due course of law; a casual or stray act of trespass does not itself displace the rightful possessor. The right should be applied in light of whether immediate assistance from public authorities is readily available. The Court relied on Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, Horam and others v. Rex, Sangappa and others v. State, and In re Mooka Nadar.

rule.if: property_offence_case and possession_not_lawfully_displaced and forcible_criminal_trespass_attempted and defenders_protected_another_persons_possession and immediate_state_protection_unavailable

predicates.property_offence_case: The proceeding concerns an alleged offence arising from a dispute over possession of property.
predicates.possession_not_lawfully_displaced: The occupant’s possession had not been ended through a lawful eviction or otherwise displaced by a valid transfer of possession.
predicates.forcible_criminal_trespass_attempted: A group entered or attempted to enter the property by force in circumstances amounting to criminal trespass.
predicates.defenders_protected_another_persons_poss: The accused intervened to protect another person who was in possession of the property.
predicates.immediate_state_protection_unavailable: The attempted forcible entry arose suddenly, without a practical opportunity to obtain immediate protection from public authorities.

issues.definition: When possession has not been lawfully displaced and defenders face a sudden forcible trespass while protecting another occupant, they may use necessary force to protect that possession.

issues.legal_issue: The appellants did not exceed their right of private defence in repelling the attempted forcible entry.
material_facts: The purchaser’s group came to assert possession after the tenant had refused to deliver the field voluntarily.
The group included a person armed with a pistol, and the appellants first asked the group to leave before using force.
The resulting injuries were held to be simple.
The courts below convicted the appellants, and the matter was an appeal against those convictions.
issues.conclusion: The appellants had not exceeded their right of private defence; the appeal was allowed, the convictions were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 99 of the Indian Penal Code limits private defence to force that is not more than necessary for the purpose of defence. The use of force must not be unduly disproportionate to the injury to be averted or reasonably apprehended and must not be vindictive or malicious. The Court relied on Jai Dev v. State of Punjab and agreed with the reasoning in Horam and others v. Rex, Sangappa and others v. State, and In re Mooka Nadar.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and private_defence_right_arose and intruding_group_was_armed and defenders_first_demanded_withdrawal and resulting_injuries_were_simple

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused appeal from convictions for offences arising out of the property incident.
predicates.private_defence_right_arose: The accused had a right to defend possession against an attempted forcible trespass.
predicates.intruding_group_was_armed: At least one member of the group attempting to assert possession carried a weapon.
predicates.defenders_first_demanded_withdrawal: The defenders asked the intruding group to leave before using force.
predicates.resulting_injuries_were_simple: The injuries caused during the incident were assessed as simple.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction concerns an armed attempted intrusion, the defenders first demand withdrawal, and the injuries are simple, the convictions are set aside and the accused are acquitted if their right of private defence arose.
